screens.title: QoS in Enterprise Switching Environments
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore Quality of Service in enterprise switching environments and why it matters for users and business-critical services. You will learn how QoS gives preferential treatment to latency-sensitive traffic like voice and video, how classification and marking allow network devices to recognize important flows, and how queuing and congestion-avoidance mechanisms keep those flows predictable under load. Imagine a busy office where voice calls and video meetings compete with large file transfers; without QoS, packets are treated equally and real-time traffic can suffer delay, jitter, or loss. We will use the DiffServ model and Catalyst QoS commands to mark and prioritize traffic, show how CoS differs from DSCP, and demonstrate practical choices for queuing—strict priority for voice, weighted scheduling for best-effort. You’ll also see the critical role of the trust boundary: if an access port doesn’t trust an IP phone’s markings, the phone’s voice will be re-marked to best-effort and lose priority. By the end of this chapter you will be able to plan, configure, and verify QoS on an access switch so voice and business apps remain reliable during congestion. Consider how your network currently handles peak load and which flows must be protected first.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives focus your practice on the skills and checks you need to implement QoS correctly on Catalyst switches. First, you will explain QoS fundamentals and why prioritizing traffic protects voice and business applications. That includes describing delay, jitter, and packet loss and how QoS reduces their impact. Second, you will differentiate between Best-Effort, Integrated Services, and Differentiated Services models, understanding when DiffServ is the practical choice for large enterprise networks. Third, you will configure Layer 2 classification and marking using CoS and Layer 3 marking using DSCP, and you will understand which marking to prefer for end-to-end policies. Finally on this screen you will start to implement queuing mechanisms and congestion avoidance. Each objective pairs a practical CLI or config task with a conceptual check so you can both perform and justify your choices. Together these four objectives prepare you to design edge marking, select queuing, and configure trust boundaries so critical flows receive predictable treatment during congestion. As you progress, compare your network’s current behavior to the desired predictable outcomes described here.

screens.title: What is QoS and why enterprise networks need it
screens.narratorSegment: Quality of Service is the network’s mechanism for giving preferential treatment to particular traffic types so those services remain reliable when links are congested. At its core, QoS addresses the symptoms of competition for limited bandwidth: delay, jitter and packet loss. Delay increases the round-trip time of packets, jitter causes variability in packet spacing that breaks real-time media playout, and packet loss forces retransmits or drops voice frames. A concrete example: consider an office during a daily backup window. Large file transfers saturate the uplink and cause packet queues to grow. Without QoS, voice packets wait in the same FIFO queue as backups and callers hear choppy audio. With QoS, voice is classified and marked at the access edge and placed into a high-priority queue on the uplink, keeping latency and jitter low. A common misconception is that QoS creates bandwidth; it does not. QoS reallocates existing bandwidth so critical flows are protected, which means less-critical flows can be delayed or dropped under peak load. The takeaway: design QoS by first identifying which applications need low latency, then ensure they are classified and given the correct forwarding behavior so user experience remains predictable. What application in your network would you protect first and why?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › What is QoS
Definition
QoS gives preferential treatment to specific traffic types to manage delay, jitter, and loss during congestion.
Delay — increased latency harms voice interactivity.
Jitter — variability in packet timing breaks real-time media.
Packet loss — causes retransmits and audio dropouts.
Key Takeaway
QoS does not add bandwidth. It reserves and schedules existing bandwidth so critical applications remain usable under load.
Office example
A daily backup saturates an uplink. Voice must be classified and prioritized so callers do not experience choppy audio.
Scenario flow
Edge: classify & mark
Core: schedule & queue
Outcome: predictable voice
This flow shows how edge marking informs core behavior. Classify at the access, mark as CoS or DSCP, then apply scheduling so voice uses a strict-priority queue on the congested link.

screens.title: QoS models: Best-Effort, IntServ, and DiffServ
screens.narratorSegment: There are three QoS models you should know and compare when designing enterprise networks. Best-Effort is the default: no special handling, packets are forwarded FIFO and congestion produces unpredictable results. Integrated Services, or IntServ, uses RSVP signaling to reserve end-to-end bandwidth for individual flows; it offers strong guarantees but requires per-flow state and signaling, which makes it impractical at scale in large networks. Differentiated Services, or DiffServ, is the model widely used in enterprises: the edge classifies and marks traffic with DSCP values, and core devices apply per-hop behaviors based on those markings without tracking flows. The practical consequence is clear: use DiffServ when you need scalable prioritization across routed domains. A common misconception is that IntServ always gives better performance; while it can provide strict guarantees, it becomes unwieldy and stateful in a large environment. Another important point is that Best-Effort is still the underlying baseline and must be managed—DiffServ merely reallocates treatment among classes. For example, in an enterprise WAN you mark voice with EF and apply expedited handling in the core; you reserve bandwidth or set strict priority queues for EF while assigning AF or default DSCP for data. The takeaway: choose DiffServ for scalable, predictable QoS and reserve IntServ for tightly controlled, small-scale scenarios where per-flow reservation is required.

keyIdea.title: Model selection
keyIdea.text: DiffServ is the practical choice for enterprise networks because it scales and relies on edge marking and simple PHBs in the core.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › QoS Models
Best-Effort
No marking or reservation. Simple but unpredictable during congestion.
When it fails: voice quality degrades under heavy load.
Integrated Services (IntServ)
Per-flow reservations using RSVP. Provides strong guarantees but does not scale well.
Misconception: per-flow always practical in large networks — not true.
Differentiated Services (DiffServ)
Edge classification and DSCP marking; core applies PHBs. Scalable and widely adopted in enterprises.
Recommended: use DiffServ for WAN QoS.
Concrete mapping
Mark voice with DSCP EF at the edge. In the core, configure expedited handling or strict priority queues for EF and use AF classes for critical data. Reserve bandwidth where needed; prefer DSCP because it persists across routers.
Check your understanding
Why is DiffServ preferred over IntServ in enterprise WANs? Because it scales by applying per-hop behaviors to marked traffic instead of maintaining per-flow state across the network.

screens.title: Classification and Marking: CoS and DSCP
screens.narratorSegment: Classification is the process of identifying which packets belong to which service class; marking is the act of tagging those packets with a QoS value the network will honor. On a switch you classify traffic using ACLs, class-maps or match conditions—common matches include DSCP values, IP addresses, or TCP/UDP ports for voice. Marking at Layer 2 uses CoS, a 3-bit field in the 802.1Q VLAN tag providing eight priority levels. At Layer 3, DSCP is a 6-bit field in the IP ToS byte and offers 64 values; DSCP is preferred for end-to-end QoS because it survives routing. A practical example: an IP phone marks voice frames with CoS 5. At the access switch, configuring mls qos trust cos tells the switch to trust that CoS value; the switch can then map CoS 5 to DSCP EF so the rest of the network sees the packet as expedited-forwarding. A common mistake is relying only on CoS across routed domains; CoS will be stripped when packets leave a VLAN, so always re-mark to DSCP at the edge for end-to-end policies. The takeaway: implement consistent classification at the edge and prefer DSCP for persistence across Layer 3 boundaries.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Classification & Marking
Classification
Identify voice, video, and mission-critical data using ACLs, class-maps, or port numbers.
Match DSCP EF or CoS 5 for voice
Match ports used by conferencing apps for video
Match IP ranges for servers or critical apps
Marking
Set CoS or DSCP via policy-map actions like set dscp ef or set cos 5.
Best practice: mark at the edge and re-mark to DSCP for end-to-end QoS.
Example: phone to uplink
Phone sets CoS 5 → access switch set mls qos trust cos → switch maps CoS 5 to DSCP EF → uplink policy prioritizes DSCP EF.
CLI pattern
# Example actions (visual only)
class-map match-all VOICE
 match dscp ef
!
policy-map UPLINK_QOS_POLICY
 class VOICE
  priority
 class class-default
  fair-queue
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
 service-policy output UPLINK_QOS_POLICY

screens.title: Configuring class-map and policy-map on Catalyst switches
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring QoS on a Catalyst switch follows a repeatable pattern: identify traffic with class-maps, define behavior with policy-maps, and apply the policy to an interface. Start by enabling QoS globally with the mls qos command. Then create a class-map to match the traffic you care about. For example, match dscp ef for voice or match access-group for specific IP ranges. Next, create a policy-map that references the class and sets actions like priority for low-latency treatment or bandwidth percent for best-effort. Finally, apply the policy with service-policy input or output on the interface. A common mistake is applying the wrong direction: classification and marking often belong on input at the access edge, while scheduling and queuing policies are applied on output of egress interfaces. For instance, you will trust CoS on an IP phone port, but the uplink should have an output policy that enforces priority for the DSCP EF-marked packets. Verification commands include show policy-map interface and show mls qos interface. Practice this pattern with the starter lab: enable mls qos, trust the phone port, create VOICE and BEST_EFFORT classes, build a policy to prioritize voice and reserve bandwidth for best-effort, and apply it to the uplink. The guided pattern prevents misapplication and ensures consistent classification and enforcement.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Configure class-map & policy-map
Terminal demo (visual)
configure terminal
hostname AccessSW1
!
mls qos
!
class-map match-all VOICE

!
class-map match-all BEST_EFFORT

  priority

Note: this block is for study and lab practice. The actual CLI should be entered in your lab device.
Common pitfall
Applying classification on output of the wrong interface or failing to trust the access port causes marked packets to be reclassified as best-effort before the uplink policy runs.
Verification commands
Use show policy-map interface <interface-id>, show mls qos interface <interface-id>, and show queueing interface <interface-id> to confirm that traffic matches and that queues behave as expected.

screens.title: Queuing mechanisms: SPQ, WRR, SRR, and WFQ
screens.narratorSegment: Queuing mechanisms determine the order in which packets are transmitted when more packets are ready to send than bandwidth allows. Strict Priority Queuing, or SPQ, always empties the highest-priority queue before servicing any lower-priority queues. This is ideal for voice but can starve lower classes if high-priority traffic is continuous. Weighted Round Robin cycles through queues, allocating service based on configured weights so each queue gets proportional bandwidth — this prevents starvation but can increase latency for the highest-priority traffic. Shaped Round Robin, a Cisco approach, blends strict priority and weighted scheduling and is commonly used on Catalyst platforms; it allows you to protect voice while providing fair access to other classes. Weighted Fair Queuing dynamically distributes bandwidth to conversations or flows for fairness, but it is less common on high-speed switch egress and more often seen on router interfaces. A practical example: configure SPQ for the VOICE class on the uplink so EF-marked packets are always sent first, and use WRR or bandwidth percent for best-effort traffic so large file transfers do not completely overwhelm other flows. A common misconception is to always use SPQ for everything; overusing SPQ removes fairness and can starve other traffic. The takeaway: match the queuing mechanism to traffic requirements — strict priority for latency-sensitive flows and weighted methods where fairness matters.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Queuing Mechanisms
Strict Priority Queuing (SPQ)
Highest priority queue always served first. Use for voice and urgent control traffic.
Weighted Round Robin (WRR)
Cycles through queues using weights so each class receives proportional service and starvation is avoided.
Shaped Round Robin (SRR)
Cisco scheduler combining priority and weighted behavior; useful on Catalyst for mixed traffic profiles.
Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ)
Provides fairness per conversation; more common on routers than on high-speed switch egress ports.
Practical example

Configure priority for VOICE class and WRR/bandwidth percent for BEST_EFFORT so voice remains low-latency while file transfers receive fair bandwidth.

screens.title: Congestion avoidance with WRED
screens.narratorSegment: Weighted Random Early Detection, or WRED, is a proactive congestion-avoidance technique that prevents queues from filling up and causing tail drops. Instead of waiting for the buffer to overflow and dropping the newest packets, WRED probabilistically drops packets as the queue depth grows based on configurable thresholds for a class. Because WRED drops are random and proportional to traffic load and priority, they signal TCP senders to reduce sending rates before queues overflow. This reduces global synchronization, where many TCP flows simultaneously back off and then ramp up together, causing repeated bursts. On Catalyst switches WRED is configured within policy-maps and applied to interfaces. A concrete example: configure WRED thresholds for best-effort traffic so when the uplink queue grows, WRED gently drops a fraction of best-effort packets while preserving EF-marked voice traffic from early drops. A common misconception is that packet drops are always bad; controlled early drops are beneficial because they maintain higher long-term throughput and reduce jitter for higher-priority flows. The takeaway: use WRED to preserve overall throughput and protect real-time traffic by dropping lower-priority packets early and randomly to avoid synchronized retransmit storms.

keyIdea.text: WRED drops lower-priority packets early and randomly to prevent tail drops and global TCP synchronization, preserving throughput and latency for priority traffic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › WRED & Congestion Avoidance
What WRED does
Drops packets probabilistically as queue depth increases to signal TCP senders early and avoid tail drops.
Prevents queue overflow and sudden loss bursts
Avoids global synchronization of TCP flows
Configured per-class with thresholds
Example configuration (visual)
policy-map UPLINK_QOS_POLICY
 class BEST_EFFORT
  random-detect
 class VOICE
  priority
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
 service-policy output UPLINK_QOS_POLICY
Here, random-detect enables WRED for the best-effort class so drops occur before the queue is full, protecting voice traffic.

screens.title: QoS trust boundary and mls qos trust
screens.narratorSegment: The QoS trust boundary defines where the network begins to trust QoS markings on incoming traffic. The guiding principle is to trust markings as close to the source as possible, typically on the access switch port connected to a trusted device such as an IP phone. On Catalyst switches you use the mls qos trust command to specify which type of marking to trust, for example mls qos trust cos to accept CoS values from an IP phone. Ports connected to untrusted endpoints, like employee PCs, should not be trusted; their markings should be ignored or re-marked to a default best-effort value. A common operational mistake is leaving a phone access port untrusted or trusting an unverified user port. In that case, the phone’s CoS 5 marking might be stripped or remapped to CoS 0/DSCP 0 before the uplink policy runs, and voice will not be matched by the uplink policy that expects DSCP EF, resulting in poor call quality despite an apparently correct uplink policy. The practical check: confirm mls qos trust on phone ports and ensure mapping from CoS to DSCP if you need end-to-end DSCP marking. Ask yourself: which physical ports in your access layer should be trusted and why?

keyIdea.text: Establish trust at access ports connected to trusted devices. Do not trust unverified user ports; otherwise device markings can be lost or remapped.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Trust Boundary
Concept
Trust markings on ports connected to trusted devices; re-mark or ignore markings from untrusted devices.
CLI example
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 mls qos trust cos
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/2
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
 # untrusted - do not use mls qos trust
What can go wrong
If the phone port is not trusted, phone CoS markings are ignored and voice may be re-marked to best-effort, so uplink policies matching DSCP EF will miss voice traffic.
Verification
Use show mls qos interface <int> to confirm trust mode and show policy-map interface to ensure traffic matches expected classes. Correct trust placement is critical for end-to-end QoS.

screens.title: Hands-on lab: AccessSW1 starter configuration
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough follows the starter code for AccessSW1, a Catalyst 9300 access switch. The objective is to enable QoS globally, trust the IP phone port, ensure the PC port is untrusted, create class-maps for voice and best-effort, build a policy with priority and bandwidth percent, apply it to the uplink, and then verify. Begin with configure terminal and hostname to identify the switch. Run mls qos to enable Catalyst QoS features. On the phone port use mls qos trust cos so CoS from the phone is accepted. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Lab: AccessSW1
Starter configuration (for lab practice)
configure terminal
hostname AccessSW1
!
# Enable QoS globally
mls qos
!
# Interface connected to IP Phone (trust CoS)
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 mls qos trust cos
!
# Interface connected to PC (untrusted)
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/2
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
!
# Class-Map for Voice
class-map match-all VOICE
 match dscp ef
!
class-map match-all BEST_EFFORT
 match dscp default
!
policy-map UPLINK_QOS_POLICY
 class VOICE
  priority
 class BEST_EFFORT
  bandwidth percent 20
 class class-default
  fair-queue
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
 service-policy output UPLINK_QOS_POLICY
end
Verification checklist
  1. show mls qos interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 — confirm trust cos
  2. show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24 — confirm classes matched
  3. show queueing interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24 — inspect queue behavior
If voice counters are zero on the VOICE class during calls, check the trust boundary and marking mapping from CoS to DSCP.

screens.title: Troubleshooting common QoS issues
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting QoS problems follows a logical sequence: confirm configuration, verify classification and marking, check trust boundaries, and inspect queuing and drops. First, confirm global and interface settings: is mls qos enabled and is the access port configured with the correct trust mode? Second, verify that classification matches expected traffic with show policy-map interface and review counters to see if VOICE or BEST_EFFORT classes have matched packets. Third, check marking: does the packet arriving at the uplink carry the DSCP value your policy expects? If not, the access switch may be re-marking or stripping CoS. Fourth, examine queuing and drops with show queueing interface and look for WRED drops or tail drops; insufficient bandwidth allocations or misconfigured queueing can cause unexpected packet loss. Common root causes include misplacing the trust boundary, misclassifying traffic (for example matching the wrong DSCP or ACL), or failing to apply the policy on the correct interface or direction. A diagnostic example: poor voice quality despite an uplink policy—inspect the access port trust setting first; an untrusted phone port is the most likely cause. The takeaway: follow the verification order and validate each step with show commands to isolate where the traffic is being altered or dropped.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Troubleshooting QoS
Diagnostic steps
  1. Confirm global QoS: is mls qos enabled?
  2. Check trust: show mls qos interface <int> to confirm trust mode on phone ports.
  3. Verify classification: show policy-map interface <int> to see matched packets.
  4. Inspect marking: ensure DSCP/CoS values on packets at the uplink match your policy.
  5. Check queueing and drops: show queueing interface <int> for WRED or tail drops.
Common root causes
  • Untrusted access port causing re-marking to best-effort
  • Incorrect class-map matches or wrong ACLs
  • Policy applied in the wrong direction or interface
  • Insufficient bandwidth allocations or misconfigured queues
Start with the trust boundary as it is the most frequent cause of prioritized traffic not matching uplink policies.

screens.title: Show commands and interpreting output
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is essential to confirm that your QoS design works under real traffic. Important commands include show policy-map interface, show mls qos interface, and show queueing interface. show policy-map interface shows per-class packet and byte counters and whether a class is matched; if the VOICE class shows zero packets during active calls, classification or marking is incorrect. show mls qos interface reveals trust settings and how CoS is handled at the access port. show queueing interface provides insight into queue occupancy, drops and whether SPQ or WRR behavior is observed. When reading counters, match the timeline: generate traffic or place a call, then run the show commands to see live matches. A common misinterpretation is seeing drops and assuming the policy is wrong; sometimes drops occur in best-effort classes because WRED is protecting higher-priority traffic — that is expected. Another useful check is to inspect the DSCP values on packets as they reach the uplink to ensure mapping from CoS took place. The takeaway: use the show commands methodically after generating relevant traffic and interpret counters in the context of your configured priorities and WRED settings.

keyIdea.text: Use show policy-map interface, show mls qos interface, and show queueing interface while generating test traffic to confirm classification, marking, and queue behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Verification Commands
Key commands
show policy-map interface <int> — shows matched class counters and actions.
show mls qos interface <int> — shows trust configuration and CoS handling.
show queueing interface <int> — inspects queue depth and drops, including WRED activity.
Interpreting output
If voice counters are observed under VOICE class during a call, classification is working. If no counters, check trust and marking. If BEST_EFFORT shows drops, check WRED thresholds and bandwidth allocation.
Run these commands while traffic is present for meaningful results. The sequence of tests helps pinpoint whether issues are at classification, marking, or scheduling stages.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the essential concepts to retain. First, QoS provides predictable performance by classifying and marking traffic at the edge and then enforcing scheduling and congestion-avoidance in the network. Second, DSCP is preferred for end-to-end QoS because it persists across Layer 3 boundaries; CoS is useful within a VLAN but must be mapped to DSCP for routed paths. Third, the trust boundary must be placed near trusted devices; failing to trust an IP phone port is a frequent cause of voice not being prioritized. Keep these ideas at the center of design and troubleshooting: mark at the edge, trust only trusted ports, and verify with show commands while generating traffic. These three practices protect voice and critical applications so they remain usable under congestion. Which one will you verify first in your network?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore Quality of Service in enterprise switching environments and why it matters for users and business-critical services. You will learn how QoS gives preferential treatment to latency-sensitive traffic like voice and video, how classification and marking allow network devices to recognize important flows, and how queuing and congestion-avoidance mechanisms keep those flows predictable under load. Imagine a busy office where voice calls and video meetings compete with large file transfers; without QoS, packets are treated equally and real-time traffic can suffer delay, jitter, or loss. We will use the DiffServ model and Catalyst QoS commands to mark and prioritize traffic, show how CoS differs from DSCP, and demonstrate practical choices for queuing—strict priority for voice, weighted scheduling for best-effort. You’ll also see the critical role of the trust boundary: if an access port doesn’t trust an IP phone’s markings, the phone’s voice will be re-marked to best-effort and lose priority. By the end of this chapter you will be able to plan, configure, and verify QoS on an access switch so voice and business apps remain reliable during congestion. Consider how your network currently handles peak load and which flows must be protected first.

These learning objectives focus your practice on the skills and checks you need to implement QoS correctly on Catalyst switches. First, you will explain QoS fundamentals and why prioritizing traffic protects voice and business applications. That includes describing delay, jitter, and packet loss and how QoS reduces their impact. Second, you will differentiate between Best-Effort, Integrated Services, and Differentiated Services models, understanding when DiffServ is the practical choice for large enterprise networks. Third, you will configure Layer 2 classification and marking using CoS and Layer 3 marking using DSCP, and you will understand which marking to prefer for end-to-end policies. Finally on this screen you will start to implement queuing mechanisms and congestion avoidance. Each objective pairs a practical CLI or config task with a conceptual check so you can both perform and justify your choices. Together these four objectives prepare you to design edge marking, select queuing, and configure trust boundaries so critical flows receive predictable treatment during congestion. As you progress, compare your network’s current behavior to the desired predictable outcomes described here.

These objectives move from understanding into hands-on skills you will use on a Catalyst access switch. First, define and configure the QoS trust boundary using the mls qos trust command so device markings from phones are honored. Second, map CoS to DSCP where appropriate and prefer DSCP for end-to-end policies because it persists across routers. Third, implement policy-maps and apply them to uplinks to enforce strict priority for voice and bandwidth guarantees for best-effort traffic. Fourth, perform verification and troubleshooting using show policy-map interface and show mls qos interface commands to confirm classification, marking, and queue behavior. Each objective includes a short CLI action and a verification step so you can validate the result. Practically, this means enabling QoS globally, trusting the phone port, creating class-maps for voice and best-effort, building a policy that prioritizes EF and reserves bandwidth, applying it to the uplink, and using diagnostic commands to confirm that voice is indeed prioritized. These skills protect real-time applications in production networks and help you quickly find misconfigurations.

Quality of Service is the network’s mechanism for giving preferential treatment to particular traffic types so those services remain reliable when links are congested. At its core, QoS addresses the symptoms of competition for limited bandwidth: delay, jitter and packet loss. Delay increases the round-trip time of packets, jitter causes variability in packet spacing that breaks real-time media playout, and packet loss forces retransmits or drops voice frames. A concrete example: consider an office during a daily backup window. Large file transfers saturate the uplink and cause packet queues to grow. Without QoS, voice packets wait in the same FIFO queue as backups and callers hear choppy audio. With QoS, voice is classified and marked at the access edge and placed into a high-priority queue on the uplink, keeping latency and jitter low. A common misconception is that QoS creates bandwidth; it does not. QoS reallocates existing bandwidth so critical flows are protected, which means less-critical flows can be delayed or dropped under peak load. The takeaway: design QoS by first identifying which applications need low latency, then ensure they are classified and given the correct forwarding behavior so user experience remains predictable. What application in your network would you protect first and why?

There are three QoS models you should know and compare when designing enterprise networks. Best-Effort is the default: no special handling, packets are forwarded FIFO and congestion produces unpredictable results. Integrated Services, or IntServ, uses RSVP signaling to reserve end-to-end bandwidth for individual flows; it offers strong guarantees but requires per-flow state and signaling, which makes it impractical at scale in large networks. Differentiated Services, or DiffServ, is the model widely used in enterprises: the edge classifies and marks traffic with DSCP values, and core devices apply per-hop behaviors based on those markings without tracking flows. The practical consequence is clear: use DiffServ when you need scalable prioritization across routed domains. A common misconception is that IntServ always gives better performance; while it can provide strict guarantees, it becomes unwieldy and stateful in a large environment. Another important point is that Best-Effort is still the underlying baseline and must be managed—DiffServ merely reallocates treatment among classes. For example, in an enterprise WAN you mark voice with EF and apply expedited handling in the core; you reserve bandwidth or set strict priority queues for EF while assigning AF or default DSCP for data. The takeaway: choose DiffServ for scalable, predictable QoS and reserve IntServ for tightly controlled, small-scale scenarios where per-flow reservation is required.

Classification is the process of identifying which packets belong to which service class; marking is the act of tagging those packets with a QoS value the network will honor. On a switch you classify traffic using ACLs, class-maps or match conditions—common matches include DSCP values, IP addresses, or TCP/UDP ports for voice. Marking at Layer 2 uses CoS, a 3-bit field in the 802.1Q VLAN tag providing eight priority levels. At Layer 3, DSCP is a 6-bit field in the IP ToS byte and offers 64 values; DSCP is preferred for end-to-end QoS because it survives routing. A practical example: an IP phone marks voice frames with CoS 5. At the access switch, configuring mls qos trust cos tells the switch to trust that CoS value; the switch can then map CoS 5 to DSCP EF so the rest of the network sees the packet as expedited-forwarding. A common mistake is relying only on CoS across routed domains; CoS will be stripped when packets leave a VLAN, so always re-mark to DSCP at the edge for end-to-end policies. The takeaway: implement consistent classification at the edge and prefer DSCP for persistence across Layer 3 boundaries.

Configuring QoS on a Catalyst switch follows a repeatable pattern: identify traffic with class-maps, define behavior with policy-maps, and apply the policy to an interface. Start by enabling QoS globally with the mls qos command. Then create a class-map to match the traffic you care about. For example, match dscp ef for voice or match access-group for specific IP ranges. Next, create a policy-map that references the class and sets actions like priority for low-latency treatment or bandwidth percent for best-effort. Finally, apply the policy with service-policy input or output on the interface. A common mistake is applying the wrong direction: classification and marking often belong on input at the access edge, while scheduling and queuing policies are applied on output of egress interfaces. For instance, you will trust CoS on an IP phone port, but the uplink should have an output policy that enforces priority for the DSCP EF-marked packets. Verification commands include show policy-map interface and show mls qos interface. Practice this pattern with the starter lab: enable mls qos, trust the phone port, create VOICE and BEST_EFFORT classes, build a policy to prioritize voice and reserve bandwidth for best-effort, and apply it to the uplink. The guided pattern prevents misapplication and ensures consistent classification and enforcement.

Queuing mechanisms determine the order in which packets are transmitted when more packets are ready to send than bandwidth allows. Strict Priority Queuing, or SPQ, always empties the highest-priority queue before servicing any lower-priority queues. This is ideal for voice but can starve lower classes if high-priority traffic is continuous. Weighted Round Robin cycles through queues, allocating service based on configured weights so each queue gets proportional bandwidth — this prevents starvation but can increase latency for the highest-priority traffic. Shaped Round Robin, a Cisco approach, blends strict priority and weighted scheduling and is commonly used on Catalyst platforms; it allows you to protect voice while providing fair access to other classes. Weighted Fair Queuing dynamically distributes bandwidth to conversations or flows for fairness, but it is less common on high-speed switch egress and more often seen on router interfaces. A practical example: configure SPQ for the VOICE class on the uplink so EF-marked packets are always sent first, and use WRR or bandwidth percent for best-effort traffic so large file transfers do not completely overwhelm other flows. A common misconception is to always use SPQ for everything; overusing SPQ removes fairness and can starve other traffic. The takeaway: match the queuing mechanism to traffic requirements — strict priority for latency-sensitive flows and weighted methods where fairness matters.

Weighted Random Early Detection, or WRED, is a proactive congestion-avoidance technique that prevents queues from filling up and causing tail drops. Instead of waiting for the buffer to overflow and dropping the newest packets, WRED probabilistically drops packets as the queue depth grows based on configurable thresholds for a class. Because WRED drops are random and proportional to traffic load and priority, they signal TCP senders to reduce sending rates before queues overflow. This reduces global synchronization, where many TCP flows simultaneously back off and then ramp up together, causing repeated bursts. On Catalyst switches WRED is configured within policy-maps and applied to interfaces. A concrete example: configure WRED thresholds for best-effort traffic so when the uplink queue grows, WRED gently drops a fraction of best-effort packets while preserving EF-marked voice traffic from early drops. A common misconception is that packet drops are always bad; controlled early drops are beneficial because they maintain higher long-term throughput and reduce jitter for higher-priority flows. The takeaway: use WRED to preserve overall throughput and protect real-time traffic by dropping lower-priority packets early and randomly to avoid synchronized retransmit storms.

The QoS trust boundary defines where the network begins to trust QoS markings on incoming traffic. The guiding principle is to trust markings as close to the source as possible, typically on the access switch port connected to a trusted device such as an IP phone. On Catalyst switches you use the mls qos trust command to specify which type of marking to trust, for example mls qos trust cos to accept CoS values from an IP phone. Ports connected to untrusted endpoints, like employee PCs, should not be trusted; their markings should be ignored or re-marked to a default best-effort value. A common operational mistake is leaving a phone access port untrusted or trusting an unverified user port. In that case, the phone’s CoS 5 marking might be stripped or remapped to CoS 0/DSCP 0 before the uplink policy runs, and voice will not be matched by the uplink policy that expects DSCP EF, resulting in poor call quality despite an apparently correct uplink policy. The practical check: confirm mls qos trust on phone ports and ensure mapping from CoS to DSCP if you need end-to-end DSCP marking. Ask yourself: which physical ports in your access layer should be trusted and why?

In the policy-map, give VOICE priority and assign 20% bandwidth to BEST_EFFORT. Apply the policy on the uplink interface with service-policy output. Troubleshooting QoS problems follows a logical sequence: confirm configuration, verify classification and marking, check trust boundaries, and inspect queuing and drops. First, confirm global and interface settings: is mls qos enabled and is the access port configured with the correct trust mode? Second, verify that classification matches expected traffic with show policy-map interface and review counters to see if VOICE or BEST_EFFORT classes have matched packets. Third, check marking: does the packet arriving at the uplink carry the DSCP value your policy expects? If not, the access switch may be re-marking or stripping CoS. Fourth, examine queuing and drops with show queueing interface and look for WRED drops or tail drops; insufficient bandwidth allocations or misconfigured queueing can cause unexpected packet loss. Common root causes include misplacing the trust boundary, misclassifying traffic (for example matching the wrong DSCP or ACL), or failing to apply the policy on the correct interface or direction. A diagnostic example: poor voice quality despite an uplink policy—inspect the access port trust setting first; an untrusted phone port is the most likely cause. The takeaway: follow the verification order and validate each step with show commands to isolate where the traffic is being altered or dropped.

Verification is essential to confirm that your QoS design works under real traffic. Important commands include show policy-map interface, show mls qos interface, and show queueing interface. show policy-map interface shows per-class packet and byte counters and whether a class is matched; if the VOICE class shows zero packets during active calls, classification or marking is incorrect. show mls qos interface reveals trust settings and how CoS is handled at the access port. show queueing interface provides insight into queue occupancy, drops and whether SPQ or WRR behavior is observed. When reading counters, match the timeline: generate traffic or place a call, then run the show commands to see live matches. A common misinterpretation is seeing drops and assuming the policy is wrong; sometimes drops occur in best-effort classes because WRED is protecting higher-priority traffic — that is expected. Another useful check is to inspect the DSCP values on packets as they reach the uplink to ensure mapping from CoS took place. The takeaway: use the show commands methodically after generating relevant traffic and interpret counters in the context of your configured priorities and WRED settings.

These are the essential concepts to retain. First, QoS provides predictable performance by classifying and marking traffic at the edge and then enforcing scheduling and congestion-avoidance in the network. Second, DSCP is preferred for end-to-end QoS because it persists across Layer 3 boundaries; CoS is useful within a VLAN but must be mapped to DSCP for routed paths. Third, the trust boundary must be placed near trusted devices; failing to trust an IP phone port is a frequent cause of voice not being prioritized. Keep these ideas at the center of design and troubleshooting: mark at the edge, trust only trusted ports, and verify with show commands while generating traffic. These three practices protect voice and critical applications so they remain usable under congestion. Which one will you verify first in your network?

Keep these concise reminders handy as you design and operate QoS. First, prefer DSCP for end-to-end policies because it persists across routed boundaries. Second, always place the trust boundary at trusted access ports and verify with show mls qos interface; misplacing it is a common cause of failure. Third, choose appropriate queuing: strict priority for voice and weighted methods for fairness, and use WRED to avoid tail drops on lower-priority classes. These three rules help you design scalable QoS policies that protect critical services.
